description: Explains every canonical CNA C API function CNA-Java does not bind. Rules are ordered and the first match wins. A bound function is never matched here: its classification is derived from the Java packages that actually reach it.

classifications.XNA_BACKING: Derived only. A bound route reached from the strict Microsoft.Xna.Framework projection.
classifications.CNA_EXTENSION_CANDIDATE: A CNA capability outside XNA 4.0. It belongs under org.openeggbert.cna.extensions, whether or not it is bound yet.
classifications.JAVA_INTERNAL_ONLY: Derived only. A bound route reached only from org.openeggbert.cna.internal plumbing.
classifications.NOT_USEFUL_IN_JAVA: A route CNA-Java must not take, because Java already owns the behaviour or the route has no Java meaning.
classifications.DEFERRED_RUNTIME: An XNA-backing route that is not bound yet. A backlog task owns it.
classifications.UNMAPPED_REQUIRES_REVIEW: Default when no rule matches. The coverage gate fails on it.

rules.reason: Vector2/3/4 arithmetic is managed in XNA and managed in CNA-Java. Routing each operation through JNI would add a per-call cost and a native failure mode the original managed API cannot produce.
Matrix arithmetic is managed in XNA and managed in CNA-Java, for the same reason as the vector family.
Quaternion arithmetic is managed in XNA and managed in CNA-Java.
MathHelper is a managed static class in XNA and a managed static class in CNA-Java.
Value-type declarations only; the header exports no callable route Java could take.
BoundingBox, BoundingSphere, BoundingFrustum, Plane and Ray intersection math is managed in XNA and managed in CNA-Java.
Color is a managed packed value in XNA and a managed packed value in CNA-Java.
The named colour table is managed constant data, already projected as Java constants.
Curve, CurveKey and CurveKeyCollection are managed XNA types with managed evaluation, already projected in Java.
The PackedVector family is managed bit packing, already projected in Java.
VertexElement and the built-in vertex value types are managed descriptors; Java builds the same descriptors before the one native declaration call.

GameComponent, DrawableGameComponent, GameComponentCollection and the service container are managed XNA behaviour. CNA-Java owns the component list and the Java Game drives it, so a parallel native component list would be a second source of truth.

Lends a fresh name for something the caller gave the lender, and a fresh name is a game child: measured in lent_effect_lifetime.c, taking one of these twice and releasing neither makes cna_game_destroy answer INVALID_STATE, and releasing both makes the same run answer SUCCESS. So a Java getter over one of these would allocate and free a native handle on every read, to hand back an object the Java facade already retains -- Skybox, ColorGradePass, PostProcessPass, ClusteredForwardEffect and RenderPipeline each keep what they were given and answer from that. The same reasoning as PbrMaterialExtensions' nine texture getters.

Lends back the identical handle the caller gave cna_render_pipeline_set_skybox -- measured, not assumed: unlike the six fresh-name getters beside it this one is the same name, so there is nothing to release and nothing a Java facade could add. RenderPipeline answers from the Skybox it was handed.

Fills a caller-provided struct with invalid handles and its struct_size/struct_version. The generated JNI adapter already writes both fields for every route that consumes these structs, as sizeof against the live header and the header's own declared version -- a compile-time value that breaks the build when the header changes, where the runtime route would absorb the change silently. CNA_INVALID_HANDLE is zero, which a fresh Java array already is.

A pure bitmask containment test over two integers the caller supplies, which java.util.EnumSet answers without crossing JNI. CNA's own bit values are pinned in probe.c by compile-time assertion against the live header, which is stronger than any runtime route could be.

Returns the CNA_ModelMeshPartHandle at the selected level. CNA-Java's LodGroup adds every level with CNA's own no-part sentinel, because the Java projection's ModelMeshPart is a managed object with no native handle -- so this route has nothing to return by construction, and selectIndex answers the level the game draws its own mesh at.

Consumes the pass handle exactly as documented, but does not decrement the game's owned-child count that the pass's own create incremented, so cna_game_destroy answers INVALID_STATE afterwards and the game cannot be closed. Binding it would give a game a route that makes it undestroyable.

CNA's engine layer (PBR materials, clustered and forward lighting, shadow families, post-processing, particles, instancing, debug drawing) has no XNA 4.0 counterpart and belongs under org.openeggbert.cna.extensions.
The extended graphics layer -- render pipeline settings, tone mapping, render and shadow quality, ASCII/CRT/dither post-process identities -- is explicitly beyond XNA 4.0.

Correct until a GraphicsDevice exists and reset by creating one: the count answers five and then zero for the same build while copy_available_ext keeps answering five, the selection becomes UNKNOWN, and the latch flag never becomes true. Measured before and after in renderer_selection.c identity mode, on a process that touches the selection at all. GraphicsRenderer.available() uses the zero-capacity probe instead of the count, and getActive() is the route that answers correctly after a device exists.

Reports the renderer this build was CONFIGURED with rather than the one running -- HEADLESS on a build configured HEADLESS, whatever CNA_GRAPHICS_RENDERER selected. Binding it would give Java a route named "current" that answers about something else. GraphicsRenderer.getActive() is bound instead and is right, and RendererCapabilities.getRendererName asks the device.
Logging, compile-time platform and renderer identity, and backend classification are CNA runtime facts XNA never exposed.
Host sensors are a CNA device extension; XNA 4.0 exposes no sensor API on the desktop profile.
Camera, clipboard, locale, power, message box, file dialog, system tray and vibration are CNA device extensions beyond XNA 4.0.
Haptic devices and effects are a CNA input extension; XNA 4.0 has only GamePad.SetVibration.
Raw joysticks with arbitrary axis, hat and trackball counts are a CNA input extension; XNA 4.0 models only the four-slot gamepad.
Text input, IME composition and the screen keyboard are a CNA input extension; XNA 4.0 exposes only Guide.BeginShowKeyboardInput.
Mouse cursor objects are a CNA input extension; XNA 4.0 exposes only Game.IsMouseVisible.
Device enumeration and hot-plug events are a CNA input extension; XNA 4.0 merges input state across devices and never enumerates them.
The .cnb container, its schemas, its writers and its loader registry are a CNA content format with no XNA 4.0 counterpart.
Remaining adapter, display-mode and presentation routes behind the bound GraphicsAdapter and PresentationParameters surface.

XNA's PacketWriter is a BinaryWriter over a growable buffer and its PacketReader is a BinaryReader over the received bytes, and the Java projection is the same. Keeping the buffer managed is what gives Position and Length exactly XNA's meaning over one cursor; a native cursor beside the Java one would be two positions to keep in step, and the packet already crosses the boundary once, at Send and Receive.

The asynchronous half of an operation the projection takes synchronously. XNA's Begin/End pair is projected over CNA's synchronous route plus CompletedAsyncResult, because CNA's asynchronous form completes before its own begin route returns; binding both would be two spellings of one operation and two places for its behaviour to drift.

Constructing or comparing a value the Java projection owns: an EventArgs built from the drained event record, a presence or quality-of-service value, a leaderboard identity, an avatar expression. These are managed values in XNA and managed values here, so their construction and equality are Java's, exactly as the vector and input value families are.

CNA's own avatar rendering and the real clip and content names behind the canonical presets. XNA's AvatarRenderer draws through the Xbox runtime and names none of this, so it is an extension rather than a member the reference API has.

Mutating a collection XNA declares read-only, or asking whether it is. The Java collection throws from every one of those members exactly as XNA's does, so no call site can exist for the native route; and a copy-out is answered from the same snapshot get and size already read.

A CLR enumerator's own lifecycle. Java's Iterator has no reset and its collections iterate by index over the same elements, so projecting a second cursor would add a handle to own and a state to keep in step for no behaviour a Java caller can reach.

A factory for an object the projection receives rather than makes, and the matching release. A gamer, a machine, a friend, an achievement and a session listing all arrive from the roster or the session that owns them, so Java never owns one to free -- and a second owner freeing a borrowed handle is the failure this classification prevents. The handles Java does own are released: JAVA-NATIVE-024 records the three that were not.

A CNA test seam: planting a roster, stamping a gamer's identity or round trip, adding a remote gamer that never connected, or counting live instances. Exposing any of it would let a consumer change what the gamer and session surface reports, which is the opposite of what that surface is for.

A second spelling of something already answered. The session's runtime type name is a C++ diagnostic string XNA's ToString does not promise, and a signed-in gamer's gamertag is the Gamer.Gamertag the base route already reads.

The host and port a discovered session was found at, and a presence line of the title's own words. XNA's AvailableNetworkSession names no address and its PresenceMode is a closed enumeration, so both belong under org.openeggbert.cna.extensions.

CNA answers membership and position for a gamer collection in one call, and Java would rather ask than walk -- but asking means declaring contains and indexOf on GamerCollection, and CLR's GamerCollection declares neither: it inherits them through IList<T>. Declaring them would put two members in the strict contract that the reference API has no counterpart for, which the full-profile gate refused. The inherited AbstractList walk stays, and it is correct.
Backs the GamerServices and Avatar families the full XNA 4.0 runtime profile declares and CNA-Java has not projected yet.
Backs the Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Net values, packet readers and writers the full XNA 4.0 runtime profile declares.
Backs NetworkSession, its discovery, its events and its rosters.
Backs NetworkGamer and LocalNetworkGamer.
The physically based material and effect family is a CNA extension beyond XNA 4.0's five stock effects.
Skinned physically based rendering is a CNA extension.
Building an effect from shader source at runtime is a CNA extension; XNA 4.0 loads compiled effect bytecode only.
Texture transforms are a CNA material extension with no XNA 4.0 counterpart.
The colour-matrix effect is a CNA extension.
Morph targets are a CNA model extension; XNA 4.0's Model has no morph data.
SkinnedModel is a CNA model extension; XNA 4.0 ships skinning only as a sample-level content processor.
Skinning data is a CNA model extension.
The animation player is a CNA model extension.
Model animation clips are a CNA model extension.
The content processor's Dictionary<string, object> side data is reachable in CNA through a dedicated handle kind that XNA exposes only as a managed object graph.
Declaring a reflectively serialized .xnb type's field list from outside the runtime is a CNA extension point.

CNA's own model loader produces a model that segfaults during teardown for any asset with a mesh part, whether the caller destroys it or leaves it to the content manager. Binding it would hand a consumer a route that kills the process, so it stays unbound until CNA is fixed.

A narrower constructor than the one the projection takes. CnaModel builds its mirror with cna_model_create_with_parents and cna_model_mesh_create_named, which carry the parent links and names an XNA model has; the defaulted and unnamed forms would lose them, and a collection built by hand would not be the model's.

CNA's model tags are an opaque C-owned pointer or a C-side dictionary. XNA's Tag is a managed object the content reader produced, which the Java projection already carries; handing a Java game a void* would be a handle it cannot use and must not free.
The setter half of CNA's opaque C-owned model tag; see the getter.

A C resource bundle with a release callback, and the two queries that read a C-owned content tag. All three hand a Java caller a void* it cannot own, and the Java model already carries its own Tag from the managed reader.

Mutating or searching CNA's mirror after it is built. The mirror exists to let CNA draw and pose an XNA model that Java owns, so the XNA graph stays the one source of truth: a part whose vertex count changed only in CNA would describe a model no Java code has. Searching a collection is a Java operation over the snapshot the graph walk already produced.
The glTF importer's diagnostics belong to a model CNA imported, which needs the content loader JAVA-UPSTREAM-004 blocks. A model mirrored from XNB carries none.
The glTF import report and its diagnostics; see the getters.

Authoring cameras and skins, posing a model from an animation clip, and the per-part primitive type, sampler state and morph data are CNA model extensions XNA 4.0 has no member for. They are read-useful only on a model CNA imported, which the blocked content loader is the way to get.
Native Model, ModelMesh, ModelMeshPart and ModelBone routes behind CNA-Java's managed XNB model graph. Binding them is how Load<Model> stops being managed-only.
Native compiled-asset reader routes behind CNA-Java's managed XNB reader.
Remaining ContentManager routes behind the bound content surface.
Remaining Effect, EffectTechnique, EffectPass, EffectParameter and EffectAnnotation routes behind the bound effect surface.
Remaining GraphicsDevice, Viewport and OcclusionQuery routes behind the bound device surface.
Remaining graphics discovery and capability routes behind the bound surface.
Remaining generic GraphicsResource name, tag and disposal routes behind the bound resource surface.
Remaining BlendState, DepthStencilState, RasterizerState and SamplerState routes behind the bound state surface.
Remaining Texture and Texture2D routes behind the bound texture surface.
Remaining Texture3D and TextureCube routes behind the bound volume surface.
Remaining RenderTarget2D and RenderTargetCube routes behind the bound render-target surface.
Remaining VertexDeclaration and VertexBuffer routes behind the bound buffer surface.
Remaining IndexBuffer routes behind the bound buffer surface.
Remaining SpriteFont routes behind the bound font surface.
Remaining SoundEffect, SoundEffectInstance, DynamicSoundEffectInstance and Microphone routes behind the bound audio surface.
Remaining AudioEngine, WaveBank, SoundBank and Cue routes behind the bound XACT surface.
Remaining media value and Song routes behind the bound media surface.
Remaining MediaLibrary, album, artist, genre, playlist and picture routes behind the bound library surface.
Remaining MediaPlayer and queue routes behind the bound player surface.
Remaining Video and VideoPlayer routes behind the bound video surface.
Remaining StorageDevice, StorageContainer and stream routes behind the bound storage surface.

XNA's input value types -- GamePadState and its four component structs, KeyboardState, MouseState, TouchLocation, TouchCollection, GestureSample and TouchPanelCapabilities -- are managed structs in XNA and managed values in CNA-Java. Their construction, equality, hashing, string form and indexing are pure value operations with an exactly specified result, so routing them through JNI would add a per-call cost and a native failure mode the original managed API cannot produce. This is the same rule the vector and matrix families carry.

XNA's dead-zone transformation is pure value math with an exactly specified binary32 result, and GamePad.GetState already asks CNA to apply it: the dead-zone mode is passed to cna_gamepad_get_state_with_dead_zone. What Java computes for itself is only the virtual thumbstick and trigger buttons XNA derives from the same transformation, which is managed there too.

A CNA test seam. Resetting the host's mouse state or stamping a packet number onto a state value is something a CNA test does to its own runtime; a Java game has no use for it, and exposing it would let a consumer change what the input surface reports.
Mouse-driven touch emulation and the real-touch-hardware query are CNA touch extensions; XNA 4.0's TouchPanelCapabilities answers only whether touch is usable, which does not distinguish the two.
Remaining shared input routes behind the bound input surface.
Remaining keyboard routes behind the bound keyboard surface. Scancode translation and key-name lookup have no XNA counterpart and are extension candidates within this family.
Remaining mouse routes behind the bound mouse surface.
Remaining GamePad capability, vibration, sensor and value-projection routes behind the bound gamepad surface.
Remaining TouchPanel, TouchCollection and gesture routes behind the bound touch surface.
Remaining Game, TitleContainer and launch routes behind the bound runtime surface.
Remaining GameWindow routes behind the bound window surface.
Remaining GraphicsDeviceManager routes behind the bound manager surface.
Remaining error-category route behind the bound diagnostic surface.
Aggregate header with no routes of its own.
Umbrella header with no routes of its own.
